title: Why do LLMs always hallucinate and will they continue to do so?
content: Researchers Sourav Banerjee and colleagues published a September 2024 paper titled 'LLMs Will Always Hallucinate, and We Need to Live With This' that mathematically proves hallucinations are inherent to large language models. The proof relies on Gödel’s first incompleteness theorem and shows that every stage of an LLM – from training data compilation to intent classification and text generation – has a non‑zero probability of producing hallucinations. Complementary work by Xu, Jain, and Kankanhalli formalises the problem with learning theory, concluding that LLMs cannot learn all computable functions and will therefore inevitably hallucinate. Empirical data corroborates the theory: Vectara’s Hallucination Leaderboard reports hallucination rates of 2.5 %–8.5 % across popular models, with some exceeding 15 % (evidence). Legal‑domain tests by Stanford RegLab found hallucination rates of 69 %–88 % for specific legal queries, with LLMs inventing over 120 non‑existent court cases (evidence). Medical‑domain studies of 10 000 hallucinations revealed systematic patterns, such as a 3.7‑fold increase in percentages ending in 5 or 0 (evidence). Even state‑of‑the‑art mitigation techniques – Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG), multi‑source RAG, and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) – can only reduce hallucinations by at most 96 %, leaving a residual 4 % that the authors argue is a mathematical floor (evidence). The authors argue that the 4 % residual is unavoidable because the halting problem and other undecidable problems persist even with perfect training and retrieval. They suggest that the focus should shift from elimination to detection, transparency, and human‑AI collaboration. A Deloitte survey cited in the article reports that 77 % of organisations are concerned about hallucinations, underscoring the practical impact (evidence). The paper concludes that while hallucinations cannot be eliminated, they can be managed within acceptable tolerance levels, such as achieving one major hallucination per 25 medical notes in clinical documentation (evidence).

title: Types of Information That Cause the Most Hallucinations
content: A Medium.com article published on October 13, 2025, identifies high-risk categories for AI hallucinations in large language models (LLMs), including obscure topics, fake citations, mathematical and logical errors, legal and medical misinformation, and speculative responses. The article outlines three primary techniques to reduce hallucinations: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), which integrates real-time access to verified external sources and has been shown to reduce hallucinations by 42–68% (up to 89% in medical applications); Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, which encourages step-by-step reasoning and improves accuracy by 35% in reasoning tasks, with a 28% reduction in mathematical errors; and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), which uses human evaluations to fine-tune models, resulting in a 40% reduction in factual errors for GPT-4 and an 85% reduction in harmful hallucinations for Anthropic’s Constitutional AI. A 2024 Stanford study found that combining RAG, RLHF, and guardrails led to a 96% reduction in hallucinations compared to baseline models. The article concludes that a multi-layered approach is essential for building trustworthy, fact-based AI systems in high-stakes environments.

title: Hallucinations: What Causes Them?
content:
Hallucinations are unreal sensory experiences that can arise from a range of causes. The article explains that while psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder with psychosis, and major depressive disorder with psychosis are common mental‑health triggers, many other conditions are responsible. General medical causes include neurological illnesses such as migraine headaches, Parkinsonism, dementias, delirium, brain tumors, and retinal infections. For example, a patient with a viral infection in both retinas reported seeing tiny people and small animals; a psychiatric consultant concluded the hallucinations were due to the eye infection, not psychosis, and the patient was reassured that no treatment was needed. Substance use disorders also frequently produce hallucinations, especially during alcohol withdrawal (delirium tremens), amphetamine use, and hallucinogens like LSD and PCP, which can generate visual, auditory, and tactile hallucinations. Certain medications—antihistamines, opiates, SSRI‑type antidepressants (e.g., fluoxetine), steroids such as prednisone, and sleeping pills—can have hallucinations as a side effect. Because general medical causes are more common than mental‑health causes, the article advises that anyone experiencing new‑onset hallucinations should see a medical doctor promptly to rule out underlying conditions.

The article also discusses normal, non‑pathological hallucinations. Bereaved individuals may see a deceased loved one, and people often experience hypnagogic hallucinations when falling asleep or hypnopompic hallucinations when waking. Children and teenagers can have self‑limited, normal hallucinations that are part of development; however, a small subset may have an increased risk of suicide, so monitoring is recommended. The article concludes that hallucinations can stem from mental‑health disorders, general medical conditions, or be normal, and emphasizes the importance of medical evaluation for new‑onset hallucinations. The article contains no sensational or biased language; it presents facts and recommendations objectively.

title: Origins of hallucinations traced to specialized brain cells
content: Researchers from the University of California at Berkeley and the Allen Institute in Seattle used laser-based neural recording and stimulation in mice to study how the brain processes optical illusions, shedding light on the origins of hallucinations. The study identified a specialized group of neurons in the visual cortex—called IC-encoder neurons—that actively fill in missing visual information, enabling the brain to perceive complete shapes, such as in the Kanizsa triangle illusion, even when no lines are present. When these neurons were stimulated without showing the illusion, mice exhibited the same brain activity as if they had seen it, indicating their role in generating perceived reality. The findings suggest that if these pattern-completing circuits become overactive at inappropriate times, they may contribute to hallucinations seen in conditions like schizoaffective disorder and schizophrenia. Lead author Hyeyoung Shin, now at Seoul National University, noted the study’s implications for understanding perception disorders, though treatments are still speculative. Dileep George of Google praised the study’s methodology, explaining that hallucinations may arise from confusion between brain predictions and sensory input. Tai Sing Lee of Carnegie Mellon University highlighted the advanced tools used to map brain-level visual processing. The research may also inform artificial intelligence, particularly in understanding how machine vision systems perceive illusions. Hallucinations are more common than believed, with a 2021 British Journal of Psychiatry study finding prevalence rates of 3% to 7% across age groups, and are linked to mental health disorders. Personal accounts from individuals like Jo Kavaliauskas and Michelle Hammer illustrate the real-life impact of hallucinations—ranging from terrifying visions to subtle, socially awkward experiences—though current medications only manage symptoms rather than eliminate them.

title: Using lightweight LLMs to cut incident response times and reduce hallucinations - Help Net Security
content: Researchers from the University of Melbourne and Imperial College London have developed a method for using lightweight LLMs to improve incident response planning and reduce hallucinations. Their approach uses a smaller, fine-tuned LLM combined with retrieval-augmented generation and decision-theoretic planning. The method works in three main steps: instruction fine-tuning, information retrieval, and planning with hallucination filtering. According to Kim Hammar, one of the authors, 'From a technical perspective, our method is deliberately designed to integrate directly into existing workflows without requiring any additional software or adaptation of existing systems.' The method has been shown to achieve shorter average recovery times, up to 22 percent faster than the best-performing frontier model tested, while also reducing ineffective actions and failed recoveries.

title: Silencing the voices? Landmark German study finds rTMS modestly effective for auditory hallucinations
content: A landmark German study published in The Lancet Psychiatry in September 2024, conducted by a consortium of seven leading German hospitals, found that repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), specifically continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS), is modestly effective in reducing chronic severe auditory verbal hallucinations in adults with schizophrenia-spectrum disorders. The study included 138 adults (43% women), with a mean illness duration of 12 years and 38% already on clozapine, the most potent antipsychotic, yet still experiencing persistent hallucinations. Participants were randomized 1:1 to active rTMS or sham (placebo) treatment, receiving 12 sessions over three weeks, targeting Wernicke’s area in both hemispheres. The primary outcome, the Psyrats questionnaire, showed a mean reduction of -6.36 in the rTMS group versus -3.74 in the sham group (p = 0.042), indicating statistically significant superiority of active treatment. Secondary outcomes revealed a significant reduction in PANSS positive symptoms, including hallucinations, but no significant differences in global functioning (GAF) or negative symptoms. Adverse events were minimal and similar between groups, primarily headaches, suggesting they were likely related to expectations rather than the treatment itself. The study’s strengths include a large sample size, rigorous blinding, multi-center design, and high treatment compliance. Limitations include a short treatment period, high dropout rates post-intervention, and lack of control over post-treatment care. The authors concluded that cTBS is a safe, well-tolerated, and effective adjunctive therapy that complements medication and psychotherapy. The author, a clinician, expressed hope that this evidence will lead to reimbursement and guideline inclusion, similar to rTMS for depression, and called for further research on cost-effectiveness and strategies to improve retention.

title: LLMがhallucinationを起こす理由　嘘を制御する方法 : 研究開発
content: Researchers Adam Tauman Kalai, Ofir Nachum, Edwin Zhang, and Santosh S. Vempala argue that language‑model hallucinations arise from the statistical objective of density estimation, which encourages confident but potentially false predictions even when training data is clean. They show that models that always output the phrase 'I don't know' (IDK) avoid errors but fail the density objective, illustrating that the pre‑training loss can produce errors despite error‑free data. The article also discusses how post‑training evaluation metrics that reward binary correctness reinforce hallucinations, because a confident wrong answer scores higher than an IDK. The authors propose that slightly adjusting evaluation incentives can reduce hallucinations. A second paper, "Can LLMs Lie? Investigation beyond Hallucination" by Haoran Huan, Mihir Prabhudesai, Mengning Wu, Shantanu Jaiswal, and Deepak Pathak, identifies neural mechanisms of intentional lying. Using logit‑lens and causal ablation, they locate specific MLP and attention heads that drive false statements, and demonstrate that intervening on these components can steer the model toward truth or lie. Experiments show that ablation of a few heads reduces hallucinations to near zero while preserving general performance. The article concludes that controlling lying requires balancing ethical concerns with practical needs, and that targeted interventions can mitigate harmful lies without impairing useful tasks.

title: How to deal with Hallucinations in Large Language models(2025 route)
content:
The article explains how to reduce hallucinations in large language models (LLMs) by adopting a multi‑layered approach. It first defines hallucinations as plausible but false outputs that arise from gaps in training data or the model’s tendency to generalise. The core mitigation strategies are: 

- 'Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (RAG)': combining the LLM’s generative power with real‑time retrieval from trusted sources to ground responses in factual content.
- 'Advanced Prompt Engineering': using chain‑of‑thought and few‑shot prompting to structure the model’s reasoning and steer it toward more reliable outputs.
- 'Guardrails and Fact‑Checking': implementing automated or human‑in‑the‑loop fact‑checking mechanisms and programmable guardrails to monitor and validate outputs in real time.
- 'Confidence and Uncertainty Quantification': leveraging the model’s self‑assessment to flag low‑confidence replies for closer scrutiny.
- 'Fine‑Tuning and Domain Adaptation': refining models on high‑quality, domain‑specific datasets to reduce errors in specialised contexts.
- 'Frequent Model Updates and Data Curation': regularly updating training data with diverse, fact‑checked sources to minimise inherited inaccuracies and bias.

The piece was published on 3 September 2025 by Medium.com.

title: AI Hallucinations: A Limitation or a Spark of Creativity?
content: Researchers are re-evaluating the concept of AI hallucinations, which occur when a model provides a convincing but fabricated response. While previously viewed as a flaw to be eliminated, some scholars suggest that hallucinations could be a creative spark. Studies have shown that a controlled increase in entropy can foster the generation of original ideas, and that hallucinations can be channeled into positive applications, such as stimulating creativity and innovation. In the medical and pharmaceutical fields, AI hallucinations are emerging as useful tools for drug discovery and biomedical design. A study on arXiv demonstrated that the inclusion of hallucinatory descriptions in prompts for language models significantly improves performance on pharmacological tasks. The research converges on a fundamental point: AI hallucinations, despite being falsehoods, can in certain contexts act as triggers for creative thinking. The goal is to broaden our understanding of AI hallucinations and to manage and harness them, rather than simply eliminating them. This requires further studies and clear precautions to avoid spreading misinformation or confusing users about the boundaries between truth and fiction. Researchers propose ethical criteria for using 'creative' AI hallucinations, such as identifying them as such and maintaining user control and awareness. The future challenge will be to design 'two-faced' AIs, capable of balancing rigorous reliability with creative vision. Ultimately, rethinking AI hallucinations does not mean ignoring their dangers, but rather recognizing that at the origin of innovative thought, there is always a 'divergent' idea.

title: Hallucinations persist partly because current evaluation methods set the wrong incentives: OpenAI on AI hallucination
content:
OpenAI’s research paper, "Why language models hallucinate," reports that GPT‑5 shows a marked reduction in hallucinations, especially during reasoning tasks, yet hallucinations still occur. The authors argue that hallucinations persist mainly because evaluation methods reward guessing over honest uncertainty. They state, 'Hallucinations persist partly because current evaluation methods set the wrong incentives. While evaluations themselves do not directly cause hallucinations, most evaluations measure model performance in a way that encourages guessing rather than honesty about uncertainty.' The paper illustrates this with a multiple‑choice test analogy: 'Think about it like a multiple‑choice test. If you do not know the answer but take a wild guess, you might get lucky and be right. Leaving it blank guarantees a zero. In the same way, when models are graded only on accuracy, the percentage of questions they get exactly right, they are encouraged to guess rather than say, 'I don't know.''

Older OpenAI o4‑mini, a compact, cost‑efficient model, performs slightly better on some metrics but has a significantly higher hallucination error rate. The paper notes that most benchmarks focus on accuracy, creating a false dichotomy between right and wrong. It says, 'When averaging results across dozens of evaluations, most benchmarks pluck out the accuracy metric, but this entails a false dichotomy between right and wrong. On simplistic evals like SimpleQA, some models achieve near 100% accuracy and thereby eliminate hallucinations. However, on more challenging evaluations and in real use, accuracy is capped below 100% because there are some questions whose answers can't be determined for a variety of reasons, such as unavailable information, limited thinking abilities of small models, or ambiguities that need to be clarified.'

OpenAI acknowledges that there is no straightforward fix; the key finding is that 'Accuracy will never reach 100% because, regardless of the model size, search and reasoning capabilities, some real‑world questions are inherently unanswerable.'
